cards.front: What should you inspect first in a punctuation question?
cards.back: Inspect the choices to identify the punctuation being tested. Then examine the relevant sentence structure. A candidate is correct only if it fits the whole sentence.

cards.front: What does CPIN stand for in the lesson?
cards.back: Colon; Period/semicolon/comma + FANBOYS; Isolated comma; No punctuation. Use it as a checking order, never as proof that a higher-priority choice is correct.

cards.front: What makes an independent clause?
cards.back: A subject and a finite verb expressing a complete thought: “The antenna receives signals.” A finite verb carries tense or follows a modal; an -ing word alone is not enough.

cards.front: Is “although the antenna receives signals” an independent clause? Why?
cards.back: No. Although makes it dependent. “The antenna receives signals” is independent; adding a subordinating word changes its status.

cards.front: Is “the antenna receiving signals from three satellites” a complete sentence?
cards.back: No. Receiving is a participle here. There is no finite main verb. “The antenna is receiving signals” is complete.

cards.front: How do you find the sentence skeleton when a subject is followed by extra information?
cards.back: Temporarily bracket a genuine nonessential insertion, then connect the subject to its main verb. “The antenna, installed last spring, receives signals” → “The antenna receives signals.”

cards.front: Can a comma alone connect two independent clauses?
cards.back: No. That produces a comma splice. Use an appropriate period, semicolon, or comma plus coordinating conjunction; a colon may work when the second part explains the first.

cards.front: When does a semicolon join clauses correctly?
cards.back: Both sides must be independent clauses. “The antenna failed; the team replaced it.” A fragment after the semicolon makes this use invalid.

cards.front: What are the two main semicolon jobs to check?
cards.back: Joining independent clauses and separating complex list items. In a complex list, the items do not need to be complete clauses.

cards.front: What does FANBOYS stand for?
cards.back: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. When one joins two independent clauses, a comma usually comes before it. Check that the second part really has its own subject and verb.

cards.front: Does “and” automatically require a comma before it?
cards.back: No. “The team calibrated the sensor and recorded the results” has a shared subject and compound predicate. Do not insert a clause-separating comma merely because and appears.

cards.front: What must come before a colon used to introduce an explanation or list?
cards.back: A complete independent clause. “The team needed one tool: a wrench.” The material after the colon explains or specifies the statement before it.

cards.front: Must the material after a colon be an independent clause?
cards.back: No. It may be a word, phrase, list, or complete clause. “The team had one concern: overheating.” The left side must still be complete.

cards.front: Why is “The required tools include: a wrench and a drill” incorrect?
cards.back: The colon separates include from its direct objects. “The required tools include a wrench and a drill” is correct. Alternatively: “Two tools are required: a wrench and a drill.”

cards.front: Why is a colon not automatically correct between two complete clauses?
cards.back: The second part must explain, identify, exemplify, or expand the first. Mere completeness on both sides does not establish that relationship.

cards.front: How do you check a dash that closes an interruption?
cards.back: Locate the opening dash and identify the entire insertion. Use a matching closing dash when the main sentence resumes. Remove the insertion to verify the skeleton.

cards.front: Can a single dash introduce an explanation?
cards.back: Yes: “The team needed one tool—a wrench.” Do not assume every dash is one half of a pair; determine whether it introduces an ending explanation or encloses an insertion.

cards.front: How do you punctuate a nonessential phrase in the middle of a sentence?
cards.back: Usually with paired commas, paired dashes, or parentheses. Both boundaries matter. “The mural, restored last year, attracts visitors.” Do not mix an opening comma with a closing dash.

cards.front: Is “I can remove it and the sentence still works” enough to prove a phrase is nonessential?
cards.back: No. Removal must also preserve the intended identification and meaning. “The paintings that survived the fire were restored” limits which paintings; deleting the relative clause changes that claim.

cards.front: How are restrictive relative clauses usually punctuated?
cards.back: No surrounding commas: “The samples that remained dry were usable.” The clause identifies a subset. Restrictiveness is about meaning; the pronoun alone is not a complete test.

cards.front: What is wrong with “The researcher, published the results”?
cards.back: The comma splits the subject from its main verb. A real insertion can occur between them, but it must be enclosed: “The researcher, after checking the data, published the results.”

cards.front: When is a comma appropriate after a dependent clause?
cards.back: A dependent clause that introduces the main clause generally takes a comma: “Although the device was old, it worked.” A following integrated clause usually does not: “It worked because the team repaired it.”

cards.front: How do you punctuate a simple three-item list?
cards.back: Use commas between items: “The kit contains tape, string, and scissors.” On SAT-style questions, inspect the whole list before deciding what the blank separates.

cards.front: Why do some lists use semicolons?
cards.back: Semicolons make item boundaries clear when items contain internal commas: “Reno, Nevada; Albany, New York; and Boise, Idaho.” Keep each entire item together.

cards.front: How do you locate the semicolon in “Ada, a chemist; Leo, a physicist; and Mei, an engineer”?
cards.back: Each item is a person plus a description. The commas connect names to descriptions; the semicolons separate complete items. Match the repeated item structure.

cards.front: When does a profession directly before a name take no punctuation?
cards.back: When the profession and name identify a single person as one integrated unit: “Biologist Mara Chen spoke.” No comma goes between biologist and Mara Chen.

cards.front: Why can “Our only guide, Mara Chen, spoke” take commas?
cards.back: Our only guide already identifies a unique person in the stated context. Mara Chen supplies supplementary naming information. This is different from an integrated profession + name.

cards.front: How do you distinguish a direct question from an indirect question?
cards.back: “Where did the team work?” directly asks and takes a question mark. “The report explains where the team worked.” makes a statement and takes a period. Judge the entire sentence.

cards.front: Can “however” connect independent clauses with commas alone?
cards.back: No. Contrastive however is not a coordinating conjunction. Use “The model was simple; however, it was accurate” or “The model was simple. However, it was accurate.”

cards.front: How does punctuation change which clause “however” belongs to?
cards.back: “The model was simple, however; it was accurate” attaches however to the first clause. “The model was simple; however, it was accurate” attaches it to the second. Read the preceding sentence to locate the contrast.

cards.front: How can you tell whether “though” is a dependent-clause starter or a parenthetical transition?
cards.back: “Though the model was simple, it was accurate” begins with a dependent clause. “The model was simple, though; it was accurate” uses parenthetical though. Determine its grammatical role.

cards.front: If a period and a semicolon are both offered, can you always eliminate both?
cards.back: No. A semicolon may separate list items, a period may require a capital letter, and the choices may include other differing words. Substitute the complete choices and check the actual structure.

cards.front: If two punctuation choices both seem grammatical, what should you check next?
cards.back: Check capitalization, list boundaries, whether an insertion closes, and which clause a transition belongs to. Do not invent a stylistic preference to break a true tie.

cards.front: What should you say to yourself before submitting a boundary answer?
cards.back: “Left side: complete or incomplete? Right side: complete clause, explanation, insertion, or list item? What exact rule permits my choice?” Name the structural reason rather than relying on a pause.

questions.text: A laboratory technician checked the freezer before leaving for the evening. Its temperature was stable ______ the backup alarm was functioning normally.
questions.reasoning: Both sides are independent clauses, so a semicolon can separate them.
wrong: A comma alone creates a comma splice.
Because cannot be followed immediately by a semicolon here.
The comma belongs before and when and joins these clauses, not after it.
questions.skeleton: Its temperature was stable / the backup alarm was functioning normally.

questions.text: The curator examined the newly acquired ______ recorded its dimensions in the catalog.
questions.reasoning: Examined and recorded share the subject the curator. The two predicate parts need no boundary punctuation.
wrong: The comma unnecessarily splits a compound predicate.
The semicolon leaves and recorded without its own subject.
The colon interrupts the coordinated predicates.
questions.skeleton: The curator examined the vase and recorded its dimensions.

questions.text: The first camera recorded visible light ______ the second camera recorded infrared radiation.
questions.reasoning: But joins two independent clauses, and the comma comes before but.
wrong: The comma is misplaced after but.
The semicolon and extra comma do not form the required comma + conjunction boundary.
A comma alone cannot join these independent clauses.
questions.skeleton: The first camera recorded visible light / the second camera recorded infrared radiation.

questions.text: To attach the panel securely, the installer needed just one additional ______ a longer bolt.
questions.reasoning: The complete statement before the colon introduces the specific component named after it.
wrong: Which begins a relative clause, but a longer bolt supplies no verb to complete it.
A longer bolt is a phrase, so it cannot stand after a clause-joining semicolon.
A boundary is needed to attach this ending explanatory phrase.
questions.skeleton: The installer needed just one additional component / a longer bolt.

questions.text: The emergency supply box ______ bottled water, a flashlight, and a battery-powered radio.
questions.reasoning: Contains takes the listed supplies as its direct objects; no punctuation separates the verb from them.
wrong: The words before the colon do not form a complete statement.
The list is not an independent clause, and the left side is incomplete.
The dash breaks the verb–object connection.
questions.skeleton: The emergency supply box contains [water, a flashlight, and a radio].

questions.text: Although the river level had fallen overnight ______ the survey team postponed its trip until the following week.
questions.reasoning: An introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma before the main clause.
wrong: Although makes the left side dependent, so a semicolon cannot join it to the main clause.
A colon needs an independent clause before it.
A comma is needed after this introductory dependent clause.
questions.skeleton: [Although the river level had fallen overnight], the survey team postponed its trip.

questions.text: The new timetable, which the transit agency released on Monday ______ includes an additional evening departure.
questions.reasoning: The comma closes the nonessential which-clause before the main verb includes.
wrong: The semicolon cannot close a comma-enclosed insertion and leaves the opening unit without its main verb.
A colon cannot replace the closing comma.
Omitting punctuation leaves the insertion unclosed.
questions.skeleton: The new timetable, [which the agency released on Monday], includes a departure.

questions.text: The observatory’s newest telescope—installed on the roof last ______ can detect objects too faint for the older telescope.
questions.reasoning: The closing dash matches the opening dash and restores telescope can detect as the sentence skeleton.
wrong: A comma does not match the opening dash.
A colon cannot close this dash-enclosed insertion.
The insertion would remain unclosed.
questions.skeleton: The telescope—[installed on the roof last winter]—can detect objects.

questions.text: At the workshop, environmental ______ presented a model of the coastal ecosystem.
questions.reasoning: Environmental scientist Leila Rahman forms one integrated identifying noun phrase.
wrong: A comma splits the identifying profession from the name and does not enclose an appositive.
A semicolon splits the subject phrase.
A colon interrupts the subject before its main verb.
questions.skeleton: Environmental scientist Leila Rahman presented a model.

questions.text: The museum’s audio guide explains how the ancient device was ______
questions.reasoning: The sentence states what the guide explains; how introduces an indirect question, so a period ends the statement.
wrong: The whole sentence is a statement rather than a direct question.
A semicolon requires an appropriate continuation; the sentence ends here.
A terminal comma leaves the sentence unfinished.
questions.skeleton: The audio guide explains [how the device was operated].

questions.text: The researchers installed monitoring stations in Bend, Oregon; Flagstaff, Arizona ______ Ithaca, New York.
questions.reasoning: Semicolons separate the city–state items, including the boundary before the final item.
wrong: A comma confuses the item boundary with the internal city–state commas.
A colon would introduce an explanation rather than a parallel final item.
The existing list uses semicolons between complete items; one is missing here.
questions.skeleton: [Bend, Oregon]; [Flagstaff, Arizona]; and [Ithaca, New York].

questions.text: Only some jars in the collection still had their original lids. The ______ were photographed before the conservation work began.
choices: jars, that retained their original lids,
jars that retained their original lids,
jars, that retained their original lids
jars that retained their original lids
questions.reasoning: The relative clause identifies the subset that was photographed and takes no surrounding commas.
wrong: The paired commas wrongly treat the identifying clause as supplementary.
The comma separates the complete subject phrase from were photographed.
The opening comma incorrectly detaches the restrictive clause and has no closing partner.
questions.skeleton: The [jars that retained their original lids] were photographed.

questions.text: The community center had exactly one volunteer coordinator. Its volunteer coordinator, Elena ______ scheduled training sessions for all new helpers.
questions.reasoning: The name is a supplementary appositive, and the comma after Park matches the existing opening comma.
wrong: Without a closing comma, the supplementary name is not enclosed.
A semicolon cannot close this comma-enclosed appositive.
A colon cannot close the appositive or precede the subjectless predicate scheduled.
questions.skeleton: Its volunteer coordinator, [Elena Park], scheduled training sessions.

questions.text: After reviewing the measurements, the engineers reached a clear ______ the support beam would need reinforcement before the structure could reopen.
questions.reasoning: The independent clause announces a conclusion; the following independent clause states what that conclusion is.
wrong: A comma alone joins two independent clauses incorrectly.
No punctuation creates a run-on.
That turns the right side into a dependent content clause, which cannot follow a clause-joining semicolon.
questions.skeleton: The engineers reached a clear conclusion / the beam would need reinforcement.

questions.text: The exhibition focuses ______ the tools used to make it rather than the finished fabric.
questions.reasoning: The preposition on must remain connected to its object, the tools.
wrong: A colon separates the preposition from its object and follows an incomplete clause.
Neither side supports a semicolon here.
The dash interrupts the required prepositional phrase.
questions.skeleton: The exhibition focuses on [the tools used to make it].

questions.text: The original sensor was bulky ______ however, the replacement fits inside a standard wristwatch.
questions.reasoning: However begins the second independent clause; a semicolon precedes it and a comma follows it.
wrong: A comma before however creates a comma splice.
No punctuation produces a run-on.
And followed directly by however, without the necessary parenthetical punctuation, does not fit this choice.
questions.skeleton: The original sensor was bulky / however, the replacement fits inside a watch.

questions.text: The scientist ______ because a storm had damaged the collection equipment.
questions.reasoning: The following because-clause gives the integrated reason for canceling; it takes no boundary punctuation here.
wrong: The comma unnecessarily detaches the ordinary following reason clause.
Because makes the right side dependent, so a semicolon is invalid.
The dependent reason clause is integrated with canceled; it is not a detached colon explanation.
questions.skeleton: The scientist canceled the trip because a storm had damaged the equipment.

questions.text: How did the designers reduce the device’s weight without weakening its protective ______
questions.reasoning: The complete sentence directly asks how the designers achieved something, so it takes a question mark.
wrong: A period does not mark this direct question.
A comma cannot terminate the complete direct question.
A semicolon cannot terminate it either.
questions.skeleton: How did the designers reduce the device’s weight?

questions.text: The kit contained three ordinary ______ a ruler, a pencil, and a notebook.
questions.reasoning: The complete clause introduces a list specifying the three items.
wrong: The items after the blank are not an independent clause.
Which begins a relative clause, but the list supplies no verb to complete it.
The list needs a boundary separating the completed statement from its specification.
questions.skeleton: The kit contained three ordinary items / a ruler, a pencil, and a notebook.

questions.text: Several fragments of pottery, recovered during the excavation and carefully cleaned by the conservation ______ evidence of trade between distant settlements.
questions.reasoning: The closing comma ends the participial insertion; provided supplies the main verb for several fragments.
wrong: The material before the semicolon lacks its main verb.
A colon cannot close this comma-enclosed insertion.
Without the closing comma, the participial insertion is not properly enclosed.
questions.skeleton: Several fragments, [recovered ... and cleaned by the team], provided evidence.

questions.text: The archive holds three annotated editions: the 1922 edition, with notes by the author; the 1948 ______ and the 1975 edition, with a chronology of the author’s life.
choices: edition; with an introduction by a critic,
edition, with an introduction by a critic,
edition, with an introduction by a critic;
edition: with an introduction by a critic;
questions.reasoning: Each edition and its description form one list item. A comma introduces the description; a semicolon ends the second item.
wrong: The semicolon splits the edition from its description and the final comma fails to mark the item boundary.
The final comma fails to match the semicolon-separated item structure.
The colon does not match the name-plus-description pattern used by the other list items.
questions.skeleton: [1922 edition, with notes]; [1948 edition, with an introduction]; and [1975 edition, with a chronology].

questions.text: Most instruments in the collection must stay indoors. The portable organ can be taken outside ______ it is regularly used at outdoor concerts.
questions.reasoning: However belongs to the middle statement, which contrasts with the indoor-only rule. The final statement supports that exception.
wrong: Attaching however to the final clause suggests a contrast between being portable and being used outdoors; those ideas support each other.
Commas alone fail to separate the two independent clauses.
However needs a comma before it when appended parenthetically to the middle clause.
questions.skeleton: Most must stay indoors. [The organ can be taken outside, however]; [it is used outdoors].

questions.text: The new battery retains a high charge after a year in storage. It therefore appears suitable for emergency equipment ______ its performance at very low temperatures remains untested.
questions.reasoning: The limitation in the final clause contrasts with the favorable assessment in the middle clause, so however begins the final clause.
wrong: A trailing however would contrast the positive middle assessment with the positive storage result; the contrast belongs before the limitation.
The comma before however creates a comma splice.
There is no valid boundary between the independent clauses.
questions.skeleton: High retained charge. [It appears suitable]; [however, low-temperature performance is untested].

questions.text: ______ the manuscript was incomplete, the editor decided that it contained enough material for publication.
questions.reasoning: Though introduces a dependent clause and stays connected to its subject and verb. The comma after incomplete closes that introductory clause.
wrong: A semicolon after though breaks the dependent-clause starter from its clause.
Though is not a parenthetical transition here, so it does not take a comma immediately after it.
A colon cannot follow the isolated subordinating word.
questions.skeleton: [Though the manuscript was incomplete], the editor decided to publish it.

questions.text: The volunteers repaired the footbridge before the festival ______ then repainted its railings to match the nearby pavilion.
questions.reasoning: The choice adds they, giving the right side its own subject and finite verb, which permits the semicolon.
wrong: A comma alone cannot join the clauses once they supplies a new subject.
And then repainted shares the original subject; the inserted comma unnecessarily separates a compound predicate.
A semicolon before and then repainted leaves a fragment after it.
questions.skeleton: The volunteers repaired the footbridge / they then repainted its railings.

questions.text: The laboratory’s revised procedure ______ reduces the risk of contamination during transport.
questions.reasoning: Matching dashes enclose the supplementary participial phrase between the subject and its main verb.
wrong: The opening dash and closing comma do not match.
The opening comma and closing dash do not match.
The colon follows an incomplete subject phrase, and the semicolon precedes a subjectless fragment.
questions.skeleton: The procedure—[developed after months of testing]—reduces the risk.

questions.text: The tiny sculptures displayed near the museum entrance ______ created from discarded electronic components.
questions.reasoning: Displayed near the museum entrance modifies sculptures. Were created is the main verb and must connect directly to that subject phrase.
wrong: The left side lacks a finite main verb and the right side lacks a subject.
The comma separates the subject phrase from its main verb.
A colon cannot follow this incomplete subject phrase.
questions.skeleton: The [tiny sculptures displayed near the entrance] were created from components.

questions.text: The city’s oldest theater, a building that has survived two major ______ reopened after a year of restoration.
questions.reasoning: The closing comma ends the entire supplementary appositive, a building that has survived two major floods. The restrictive that-clause stays inside that appositive.
wrong: The opening appositive comma would have no closing partner.
A semicolon cannot close the comma-enclosed appositive; the sentence skeleton still needs reopened.
A colon cannot close this insertion or follow a unit lacking its main verb.
questions.skeleton: The theater, [a building that has survived two major floods], reopened.

questions.text: The map identified three sampling sites: the marsh near the river, which flooded each spring; the meadow beside the ______ and the woodland behind the laboratory, which remained shaded all day.
questions.reasoning: The semicolon separates the second site from the third site in the complex list; the meadow item itself needs no internal comma.
wrong: A period breaks the list and leaves the and the woodland continuation as a fragment.
A comma fails to preserve the established semicolon item boundaries.
A colon falsely makes the woodland an explanation of the meadow.
questions.skeleton: [marsh, which flooded]; [meadow beside the reservoir]; and [woodland, which remained shaded].

questions.text: A new program makes the collection available to remote visitors ______ digital reproductions of every item can now be viewed on the museum’s website.
questions.reasoning: Both sides are independent clauses. A semicolon works with lowercase digital; the period choice leaves the new sentence uncapitalized.
wrong: After a period, Digital would need a capital D.
A comma alone creates a comma splice.
No punctuation creates a run-on.
questions.skeleton: A program makes the collection available / digital reproductions can be viewed online.

questions.text: The carpenter’s assessment had one clear ______ both the frame and the door needed replacement before the building could reopen.
questions.reasoning: The complete left clause announces an implication, and the following complete clause explains exactly what that implication is.
wrong: That makes the right side dependent, so it cannot follow a clause-joining semicolon.
The comma alone joins two independent clauses and creates a comma splice.
No punctuation creates a run-on between the independent clauses.
questions.skeleton: The carpenter’s assessment had one clear implication / both the frame and the door needed replacement.

questions.text: During the lecture, historian Nia ______ described how merchants used the river to transport goods.
choices: Okafor, a specialist in regional trade,
Okafor a specialist in regional trade
Okafor; a specialist in regional trade,
Okafor, a specialist in regional trade
questions.reasoning: Historian Nia Okafor is integrated, while the supplementary description following the name needs paired commas.
wrong: The supplementary noun phrase is not enclosed.
The semicolon splits the subject from its main verb and begins a fragment.
The description has an opening comma but no closing comma before described.
questions.skeleton: Historian Nia Okafor, [a specialist in regional trade], described the trade routes.
